title: The Tavern of One Bartender
subtitle: Async and the Event Loop
flavor: One bartender. One pair of hands. Every patron in this tavern is served through them — that bartender is the event loop, and tonight you are it. For each order choose: park it, do it, or hand it to the kitchen. Then the ticks fall, and the ledger does not lie.

rounds.name: A Quiet Evening
rounds.intro: Three patrons, one bartender. Learn your three moves before the rush comes.

orders.name: Ale from the Deep Cellar
orders.desc: Open the tap and the great keg pours on its own. Someone must hand the mug over when it is full.

orders.name: Split a Coin Pouch
orders.desc: Two brothers, one pouch. A single tick of honest counting.

orders.name: Grind the Widow's Beans
orders.desc: Six ticks of hard grinding. Whoever grinds, grinds — no magic shortens it.

rounds.teach: The bartender is an event loop: ONE pair of hands that every patron shares. I/O work (the ale) pours itself — AWAIT parks it, the kernel does the waiting, and the loop pays a single tick to serve it when the bell rings. CPU work (the grinding) has no background to run in: hands must do it, and the only choice is whose — yours, freezing the whole bar, or the kitchen's, in parallel, for a fixed handoff price.

rounds.name: The Supper Rush
rounds.intro: Five orders land at once. Every tick your hands are busy, EVERY patron pays for it.

orders.name: Ladle the Simmering Stew
orders.desc: The pot simmers over its own fire. Standing there watching it helps no one.

orders.name: Balance the Merchant's Ledger
orders.desc: Five ticks of pure arithmetic, and the merchant watches your quill.

orders.name: Wipe a Spilled Tankard
orders.desc: One quick wipe. Faster done than delegated.

orders.name: Uncork the Cellar Wine
orders.desc: Once opened, it breathes on its own down in the dark.

orders.name: Knead the Night Loaves
orders.desc: Seven ticks of heavy kneading. The dough does not care whose arms ache.

rounds.teach: Under load the rule shows itself: whenever the loop is busy, every unserved patron drains at once — latency on a blocked loop is shared pain. Parking I/O keeps the bar open for almost nothing; the kitchen keeps long CPU work off your hands for a fixed handoff price. And watch the pass: even a free bartender serves ONE completion per tick — an event loop gives you concurrency by interleaving, never two things literally at once.

rounds.name: Festival Night
rounds.intro: Seven orders, two cooks, one impatient Baron. Festival night is production traffic.

orders.name: Roast on the Turning Spit
orders.desc: The spit turns itself over the fire. Eight ticks until the fat stops spitting.

orders.name: Grind the Festival Spice
orders.desc: Six ticks of pestle work for the crowd's cups.

orders.name: Flip the Twins' Coin
orders.desc: One tick to settle the bet before fists do.

orders.name: Mull the Harvest Cider
orders.desc: It steeps on its own; rushing it ruins it.

orders.name: Carve the Roast Boar
orders.desc: Five ticks of knife work, and it cannot be rushed either.

orders.name: A Toast for the Baron — NOW
orders.desc: Two ticks of flourish. The Baron grants you six ticks of patience and not one more.

orders.name: Draw the Midnight Mead
orders.desc: The old cask gives it up slowly, all by itself.

rounds.teach: Festival night is production load: many small completions, a few heavy jobs, one client with a tight deadline. The judgment calls: AWAIT on I/O is nearly free, so it is almost always right; the kitchen charges a fixed handoff, so it pays only when the work outweighs the overhead — the Baron's two-tick toast was faster done at the bar; and there were only two cooks — pools are finite, so a worker wasted watching liquid pour makes real CPU work queue behind it.

tiers.line: A flawless night — every patron served, every bell answered. You think like a scheduler. Read the ledger anyway: even a perfect score can hide a cook wasted watching a pour.
The tavern roars your name. A few ticks slipped away — read the timeline and find where.
Half the room went home fed. Study the red ticks: every one of them is a patron's patience you spent.
The tavern stands empty and the floor is sticky with waste. Read where the time went — the loop forgives nothing, but it always shows its ledger.

endcard.title: The Bartender's Ledger
lines: AWAIT = asynchronous I/O. The kernel does the waiting in the background; the loop stays free; the only loop cost is the resume — the callback — when the result is ready.

SEND TO KITCHEN = a worker pool (threads or processes). Parallel hands for CPU-bound work, bought with a fixed handoff overhead — never worth it for tiny tasks, and wasted on I/O the loop could simply await: the worker would only stand and wait.

DO NOW = running it on the event loop. Right only for genuinely tiny work. Anything long — CPU grinding or synchronous I/O — blocks the loop, and one blocked loop stalls every request in the process. That is the one unforgivable sin.

The fine print, in Python: the GIL keeps CPython threads from running Python CPU work in parallel, so heavy CPU wants a process pool — which also pays to serialize its arguments. The one honest kitchen use for I/O is a blocking-only library with no async client: wrapping it in a thread (asyncio.to_thread) beats blocking the loop.
